To sabotage something means to deliberately damage, weaken, or ruin it so that it fails — and usually to do so in a hidden or sneaky way.

The key word here is deliberately. Sabotage is never an accident. Someone who sabotages something has a goal: to make that thing stop working, fall apart, or not succeed.

This is a powerful and flexible word. You can sabotage almost anything:

Physical things — A spy might sabotage a factory by breaking its machines so it can't produce weapons.

Plans and projects — A jealous colleague might sabotage your project by hiding important files or giving you wrong information, so your work fails.

Relationships — A manipulative person might sabotage their friend's new romance by spreading lies about that friend to their partner.

Opportunities — Someone might sabotage your job interview by giving you the wrong time on purpose, making you arrive late.

Efforts and goals — A competitor might sabotage your business by secretly spreading bad rumors about your products.
The Two Most Important Features of Sabotage

1. It is always intentional.
If someone accidentally knocks over your work and ruins it, that is not sabotage. Sabotage requires a choice — a deliberate decision to cause harm or failure. The person doing it knows exactly what they are doing and why.

2. It often happens secretly or from a hidden position.
The saboteur (the person sabotaging) usually pretends to be neutral, helpful, or uninvolved. They work against something while appearing not to. This hidden quality is what makes sabotage especially damaging and hard to detect. It's a kind of betrayal.

People sabotage things for many different reasons:

  • Jealousy — they don't want someone else to succeed
  • Resentment — they feel wronged and want revenge
  • Competition — they want to win, so they weaken the competition
  • Opposition — they disagree with something and want to stop it
  • Fear — they are afraid of what will happen if something succeeds

The motive matters because sabotage is not random destruction. It is strategic. The saboteur targets something specifically because of what it represents or what its success would mean.

Sabotage doesn't always mean breaking or destroying something physically. It has two forms:

Active sabotage — You do something harmful to cause failure.

Example: A disgruntled employee deletes important company files before quitting.

Passive sabotage — You deliberately do nothing when you should act, causing failure through inaction.

Example: A teammate "forgets" to pass along critical information so your presentation goes wrong.

Both are sabotage because both involve a deliberate choice to cause harm.
Self-Sabotage — A Special and Important Case

One of the most powerful uses of this verb is when the subject and the victim are the same person:

"She sabotaged herself." or "He kept sabotaging his own success."

This is called self-sabotage, and it means a person is unconsciously (or sometimes consciously) doing things that ruin their own chances, goals, or happiness.

Someone who deeply fears failure might self-sabotage by procrastinating until it's too late — essentially guaranteeing the failure they feared, but on their own terms.

Someone who doesn't feel they deserve love might self-sabotage a good relationship by picking fights, pulling away, or behaving in ways that push their partner out.

Self-sabotage is unique because there is no outside enemy — the person is working against themselves, often without even realizing it. It is frequently driven by fear, low self-worth, or a subconscious belief that success or happiness is dangerous or undeserved.

"Sabotage" is a strong, serious word. It carries a tone of betrayal, strategy, and malice. When you use it, you're saying:

  • This was not a mistake
  • This was not careless
  • Someone meant for this to fail

It's a more intense word than simply "ruin" or "damage." If you say "the storm ruined the event," that's neutral — nobody is to blame. But if you say "someone sabotaged the event," you are pointing at deliberate, human wrongdoing.
Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Imagine a race. You're in the lead. Your opponent, instead of running faster, sneaks over and quietly deflates your tires before the race begins — then walks back to the starting line, smiling innocently.

That is sabotage. Hidden. Deliberate. Targeted. Designed to make you fail without you even knowing what happened or who did it.

To sabotage is to deliberately and often secretly undermine, damage, or destroy something — or someone's efforts — so that it fails. The act is always intentional, usually motivated by jealousy, resentment, competition, or fear, and can be directed outward at others or inward at oneself.
